text: Every chapter before this one configured what an agent sees — Incident, Problem, Change, and Request forms in Classic UI or UI16. Service Portal is the opposite front door: a branded, end-user-facing self-service website callers use without ever touching an agent workspace.

Classic UI renders server-side forms and list views for agents working tickets. Service Portal, reachable at a URL like slash sp, is a client-side AngularJS application — cards and forms styled like a modern web app. A Business Rule written for the Classic UI Incident form doesn't automatically behave the same way on a Service Portal page, because the two surfaces don't render the same way at all.

Service Portal configuration has exactly three layers. A Portal record is the overall site — its URL suffix, its default Homepage, and which Theme it applies. A Theme carries portal-wide branding and CSS, applied to every page at once. And a Page is one routable URL inside that portal — the Homepage, the Service Catalog, a Knowledge Base search page — each holding the widgets placed on it.

Change a Theme once, and every page in that portal picks up the new look without touching any individual page's configuration. That separation — what a page shows, versus how everything looks — is the entire point of giving Theme its own record, separate from Portal and Page.

Under the hood, Service Portal runs on AngularJS — specifically Angular 1 point x. That's why you'll see double-curly interpolation like data dot title, and directives like ng-repeat written as HTML attributes, starting in the next lesson. It's a real, if dated, front-end framework, not server-rendered HTML forms.

Service Portal isn't a replacement for Classic UI — agents still work tickets in the workspace. And it isn't ServiceNow's newest direction either: UI Builder, building Next Experience portals, is the modern, drag-and-drop alternative ServiceNow now steers new builds toward. Service Portal remains real and extremely common in production, which is why this course teaches it. Next up: the widget, the real building block placed on every portal page.
